Venkateswara of Tirupati

Temple Stories

Venkateswara of Tirupati

The story of Srinivasa and Padmavati — the Lord of the Seven Hills

In everyday English — from the Varaha Purana and the Venkatachala Mahatmyam

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This is a temple story — but first it is a family story. A quarrel between husband and wife, a mother's love, and the preparations for a wedding — the same things that happen in our own homes, in the world of the gods. Where there is love, read softly; where the wedding is celebrated, let joy into your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Bhrigu grave, Vishnu calm, Lakshmi furious, Vakula Devi full of a mother's love.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is from the Varaha Purana and the Venkatachala Mahatmyam — the temple's own telling of its story. Where the tellings differ, each difference is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From, in its own box — and the beloved local story of the cow is in a box of its own too, never mixed into the main story.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Vishnu / Srinivasa — the Lord of Vaikuntha. In Vaikuntha he is sky-blue, four-armed, wearing a tall gold crown with a peacock feather and a yellow pitambara. On earth, on the Venkata hill, he is Srinivasa — deep dark blue-black, a tall gold crown, conch and discus in his upper hands, his lower right hand giving a blessing, his lower left hand on his hip, and a great white namam on his face — with a red mark in its centre — beneath which his eyes are barely visible.

Lakshmi — Vishnu's wife, goddess of wealth and good fortune. Fair warm skin, a red saree with a gold border, a tall gold crown — with no peacock feather — a pink lotus in her hand.

Bhrigu — the great sage whose test begins this story. A white beard, saffron robes, a kamandalu in his hand.

Padmavati — daughter of King Akasha Raja, the girl found in a lotus. She looks like Lakshmi — fair skin, a red saree — but she is Padmavati, not Lakshmi.

King Akasha Raja — king of Narayanavanam, Padmavati's father. Queen Dharanidevi is his wife.

Vakula Devi — the elderly woman who lives on the hill, Srinivasa's mother. In a previous birth she was Yashoda — Krishna's foster mother.

Narada — the divine sage who travels everywhere bringing news and reading palms. A white beard, a veena in his hand.

Kubera — treasurer of the gods. Pot-bellied, wearing gold jewellery, with a treasure pot and a money bag beside him.

Brahma — creator of the worlds. Four faces, a long white beard, seated on a pink lotus. Shiva — ash-white skin, a crescent moon in his topknot, a snake around his neck, a trishul in his hand. Both stand as witnesses at the wedding.

Adisesha — the serpent on whom Vishnu reclines in Vaikuntha. They say the same serpent lies on earth as the Seshachalam hills.

1 · Bhrigu's Test · · BHRIGU TESTS THE TRIMURTI

This happened long ago. The sages were performing a great yajna. When it was done, a question arose — to whom should the fruit of the yajna be given? To Brahma, to Vishnu, or to Shiva? Who is the greatest of the three?

The sages said — “No ordinary man can decide this. Sage Bhrigu will go — he will test all three and tell us.”

Bhrigu went first to Brahma. Brahma sat with Sarasvati — lost in his own thoughts. He did not even look toward Bhrigu. Bhrigu returned in silence.

Then he went to Shiva. Shiva sat with Parvati — deep in his own meditation. He too could not see Bhrigu. Bhrigu returned from there as well.

At last Bhrigu went to Vaikuntha — Vishnu's world. There Vishnu lay on Adisesha, Lakshmi seated beside him. Vishnu was asleep — he did not even know Bhrigu had come.

Bhrigu grew angry. “I am a sage of the three worlds — and no one even looks at me!” — and in his anger he kicked Vishnu on the chest.

But Vishnu did not grow angry. He sat up — and took Bhrigu's foot in his own hands.

Vishnu said — “O sage, has your soft foot been hurt by my hard chest? Come, let me press it for you.”

And as he spoke, he pressed away an eye that stood in the sole of Bhrigu's foot — they say that eye was the sage's pride.

Bhrigu's eyes opened. The god in whom there is such humility — he is the greatest. He returned to the sages and said — “Give the fruit of the yajna to Vishnu.”

Pause and think — Bhrigu kicked — and Vishnu pressed his foot. Is that what it means to be great — to answer a blow not with a blow, but with kindness? And the eye in the sole of Bhrigu's foot — is pride also like an eye, showing us only our own greatness?

2 · Lakshmi's Anger · · LAKSHMI'S ANGER

But one person who had seen all this could not stay silent — Lakshmi.

The chest that was kicked — that chest was Lakshmi's home. She dwells on Vishnu's chest. The kick landed on her own abode — and her own husband apologised to the man who kicked it!

Fire rose in Lakshmi's heart. “My abode has been insulted — and my husband stayed silent?”

Lakshmi said — “I will not stay here any longer. What is the use of staying with one who will not stand up for his wife's honour?”

And Lakshmi left Vaikuntha and came down to earth. She went to Karavirapura — which today is called Kolhapur — and began a long penance there.

In Vaikuntha, Vishnu was left alone. Vaikuntha without Lakshmi did not feel like Vaikuntha. He came down to earth to search for her.

He wandered from the foothills of the Himalayas to the banks of the Ganga, from the Vindhya hills to the plains of the south — but Lakshmi was nowhere to be found.

At last he came to the Seshachalam hills of the south. Their air, their trees, their peace — everything felt like Vaikuntha. Vishnu thought — “I will stay here. Perhaps she will be found here.”

Pause and think — Lakshmi grew angry — but her anger was not only for herself; it was for the insult to her home. Can anger ever be right? And Vishnu — the Lord of all — why did he wander the whole earth searching for his wife? Does love make even the greatest small?

3 · Srinivasa on the Venkata Hill · · SRINIVASA ON THE VENKATA HILL

The Seshachalam hills — they say these hills are Adisesha himself, lying in the form of a serpent. His seven hoods — seven hills. One of them is the Venkata hill.

Vishnu came to the Venkata hill and began to live in an anthill — beneath a tamarind tree, beside the Pushkarini, the holy pond. No palace, no throne — only the anthill, the tree and the pond.

On that same hill lived an elderly woman — Vakula Devi. She saw Srinivasa — and kept him with her like a mother. They say Vakula Devi was Yashoda in a previous birth — Krishna's foster mother — who had not had the fortune of seeing Krishna's wedding. Krishna had given her a boon — “In your next birth you will be my mother and see my wedding.”

Srinivasa now lived as Vakula Devi's son. On the hill he did penance, bathed in the pond, and waited for Lakshmi to return.

The Cow and the Anthill — a Beloved Local Telling

A much-loved local story of Tirupati says that Brahma and Shiva took the forms of a cow and a calf, so that milk would reach Srinivasa. Every day the cow came to the anthill and poured her milk over it. One day the cowherd saw this — and in anger raised his axe. Srinivasa came out of the anthill and stood before the cow, taking the blow upon himself. The cowherd fell down in fright at the sight. This story is dearly loved in the temple's local tradition — but it is not the main Puranic story, so we have not mixed it into the main telling. The tellings also differ on whether the blow fell on his chin or on his head.

Pause and think — Vishnu — who had all the splendour of Vaikuntha — went to live in an anthill. Does love make even the greatest choose a small home? And Vakula Devi — an ordinary elderly mother — became the mother of God. Is a mother's love also a kind of devotion?

4 · The Girl Found in a Lotus · · THE GIRL FOUND IN A LOTUS

Meanwhile, not far from the hill, King Akasha Raja ruled at Narayanavanam. He had everything — but no child.

One day the king was ploughing a field with a golden plough, preparing for a yajna. The plough moved through the earth — and suddenly a lotus bloomed out of the soil. In the middle of the lotus — a tiny baby girl, asleep!

The king lifted the child — and a voice from the sky said — “O king, she is your own daughter. Raise her.” The king placed the baby in the lap of Queen Dharanidevi.

Found in a lotus — so she was named Padmavati. She is also called Alamelu Manga — the goddess born in lotus petals.

Padmavati grew up — beautiful, gentle, soft as a flower. One day Sage Narada came to her and looked at her palm.

Narada said — “Princess, the lines of your hand say — your marriage will be with Vishnu himself.”

One day Srinivasa came hunting into the garden — and there he saw Padmavati picking flowers with her maids. They looked at each other — and love woke in both their hearts.

Padmavati returned to the palace — but her heart stayed behind in the garden. Without Srinivasa she grew restless — food did not please her, sleep did not come.

Pause and think — Padmavati was found in a lotus in the earth — as if the earth itself had handed her to the king. Is what we find sometimes greater than what we ask for? And Narada read her palm and told the future — is telling the future also a kind of responsibility?

5 · Preparing for the Wedding · · PREPARING FOR THE WEDDING

Srinivasa returned to the hill — but his heart too had stayed behind in the garden. He told Vakula Devi everything — and showed her his true form. “Mother, I am Vishnu himself — and you are my Yashoda, my mother.”

Tears came to Vakula Devi's eyes — her boon was about to be fulfilled. She was going to see her son's wedding with her own eyes.

In the palace, Padmavati had fallen ill — restless with love. Then a fortune-teller came — Srinivasa himself in disguise — and said to Padmavati — “Princess, you were born to marry Vishnu. Do not worry — he will come.” Padmavati's heart grew calm.

Vakula Devi wrapped her shawl around herself and went to the court of King Akasha Raja — and asked for Padmavati's hand for her son Srinivasa.

Vakula Devi said — “O king, my son Srinivasa wishes to marry your daughter.”

The king said — “I am glad — but I have one condition. My son-in-law cannot be poor. Srinivasa must bear the whole expense of the wedding.”

The king agreed. His adviser Brihaspati wrote the wedding invitation. Srinivasa called a council of the gods — and asked their consent for his marriage. All the gods rejoiced.

But there was one great problem — Srinivasa had no wealth. Where would a young man living on a hill find the money for a princess's wedding?

Pause and think — Vakula Devi — an ordinary mother — went to the king's court to ask for a bride for her son. Is a mother's love the greatest courage of all? And the king's condition — is a condition of wealth right in a marriage, or should there be a condition of love?

6 · The Loan from Kubera · · THE LOAN FROM KUBERA

Srinivasa had no treasure. He went to Kubera, the treasurer of the gods.

Srinivasa said — “Kubera, I need wealth for the wedding. I take a loan from you — and I promise I will repay your money.”

Kubera gave a great sum — pots filled with gold coins. Srinivasa wrote a promissory note with his own hand — that he would repay the loan. And as witnesses stood Brahma himself and Shiva.

The promise was this — the interest on the loan would be repaid through the whole Kali Yuga, and the principal at the dawn of the next yuga. They say that is why, even today, whatever devotees place in the hundi of the Tirupati temple is counted as an instalment of Srinivasa's loan.

They say the copper plates on which this loan is believed to be written are still kept in the museum at Tirumala.

The Amount of the Loan — the Tellings Differ

On how much was borrowed, the tellings do not agree. Some say fourteen lakh Ramamudra coins, others say one crore and four lakh coins. The difference in amount does not change the heart of the story — God took a loan for his wedding, and it is repaid through the offerings of devotees.

Pause and think — God himself took a loan — for a wedding! Does this story teach us that asking is also sometimes devotion? And what devotees place in the hundi — is it a donation, or a help to God?

7 · The Wedding · · THE WEDDING

The wedding day came. At Narayanavanam there was the scent of flowers, the light of lamps, the sound of music — everything was adorned.

Srinivasa became the bridegroom — a tall gold crown, a yellow pitambara, garlands around his neck. Padmavati became the bride — a red saree, gold jewellery, a wedding garland in her hands.

Brahma and Shiva themselves came to the wedding — to bless. Gods, sages, gandharvas — all were present. Vakula Devi saw her son's wedding with her own eyes — her boon was fulfilled.

Padmavati placed the garland around Srinivasa's neck — and Srinivasa placed one around Padmavati's.

Conches sounded, flowers rained down — and the gods in the sky cried out in joy.

After the wedding, Lakshmi too returned. They say that now both are on Srinivasa's chest — Lakshmi on one side, Padmavati on the other — both his wives, both his strength.

And then Srinivasa promised — “I will stay here through the whole Kali Yuga — on this hill — so that every devotee who comes may have my darshan.” They say that from then on he stands on the Venkata hill in the form of a stone idol.

Pause and think — Brahma and Shiva stood as witnesses at the wedding — the greatest gods, witnesses to a marriage. Is a wedding only about two people — or about the whole family and community? And Lakshmi's return — is the return of one who was angry the greatest joy of all?

8 · The Self-Manifested Idol · · THE SELF-MANIFESTED IDOL

In the sanctum of the Tirumala temple — called Ananda Nilayam — Srinivasa stands. No one made this idol — it is swayambhu — self-manifested.

The idol is about eight feet tall — of black stone — facing east. On his face is the great white namam — with a red mark in its centre — beneath which his eyes are barely visible. They say God's eyes are so kind that seeing them directly would overwhelm a devotee's heart — so the namam covers them.

On his chest are two small goddesses — Lakshmi and Padmavati — as in the story, so in the idol.

This temple is one of the eight swayambhu shrines of Vishnu — and one of the 108 Divya Desams, the temples whose glory the Alvar saints sang.

The temple stands on the southern bank of the Swami Pushkarini pond. They say Adi Varaha — who lifted the earth out of the ocean — was already present on the pond's western bank. First the darshan of Varaha, then of Srinivasa — that is the tradition.

Pause and think — No one made the idol — it appeared by itself. Does that mean God does not need to be called — he comes himself? And the idol's eyes are covered by the namam — is hiding also sometimes kindness, even in darshan?

9 · Tirupati Today · · TIRUPATI TODAY

Today Tirupati — in Andhra Pradesh, on the hills of Tirumala — is one of the greatest pilgrimages in the world.

There are seven hills — Seshadri, Neeladri, Garudadri, Anjanadri, Vrushabhadri, Narayanadri and Venkatadri. They say all seven are the seven hoods of Adisesha. The temple stands on the seventh hill — Venkatadri.

Devotees climb the hill — many on foot, many by the steps — chanting “Govinda! Govinda!” Below is the town of Tirupati, above is Tirumala — and between them the hill path.

In the temple the darshan lasts only a few moments — the crowd keeps moving forward — but in those few moments devotees see what the story tells — deep dark blue-black Srinivasa, the great white namam, the blessing hand.

Before the temple stands the great hundi — devotees place money, gold and flowers in it — as if repaying an instalment of Srinivasa's loan. And as prasad they receive the famous Tirupati laddu.

At the foot of the hill, at Tiruchanoor, stands Padmavati's own temple — they say first her darshan there, then Srinivasa's on the hill.

And so — a story that began with a kick — reaches the Lord who stands upon seven hills.

Pause and think — Lakhs of devotees climb the hill every year — for a darshan of only a few moments. Is the worth of a darshan measured by its length — or by its feeling? And a single coin placed in the hundi — does it too become part of the story?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Sources

The main story of this book is from the Varaha Purana and the Venkatachala Mahatmyam, together with the Bhavishyottara Purana. The official temple legend of the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) rests on these same texts.

Where the Venkatachala Mahatmyam Is Found

The Venkatachala Mahatmyam is held to be part of the Skanda Purana's second book — the Vaishnava Khanda. Some sources place it in the Bhavishyottara Purana as well. TTD calls it a collection of about eleven thousand verses drawn from several Puranas — so this book does not name any single text as the only source.

In the Bhagavata, Bhrigu's Story Is Different

In the Bhagavata Purana (Tenth Canto, Chapter 89) the story of Bhrigu's test is told differently — there Vishnu rises together with Lakshmi and apologises to Bhrigu, and Lakshmi does not leave in anger. Lakshmi's anger and her coming to earth belong to the Venkatachala Mahatmyam, not to the Bhagavata. We have followed the Mahatmyam's telling, because that is the temple's own story of Tirupati.

Who Is Padmavati

On this the tellings do not agree. Some say Padmavati is herself an incarnation of Lakshmi — born on earth as Lakshmi. Some say she is the incarnation of Vedavati — who in the Treta Yuga did penance and asked Rama for marriage. And some hold her to be a second wife, distinct from Lakshmi. In this book the main story calls her the daughter of King Akasha Raja and the wife of Srinivasa — and tells Lakshmi's return separately — because that is the form of the temple's telling.

The Cow and the Anthill — a Beloved Local Telling

Brahma and Shiva becoming a cow and a calf, the cow pouring her milk over the anthill, the cowherd's axe, and Srinivasa taking the blow upon himself — this is a much-loved story of Tirumala's local tradition, and it appears in the temple's own telling (TTD's temple legend) too. We have kept it in a box of its own, apart from the main story — because it is a local tradition's story, not the main Puranic stream.

The Amount of the Loan — the Tellings Differ

On how much was borrowed, the tellings do not agree. Some say fourteen lakh Ramamudra coins, others say one crore and four lakh coins. All the tellings agree on the promise — the interest through the Kali Yuga, and the principal at the dawn of the next yuga.

Varaha and the Pushkarini

According to the Varaha Purana, Adi Varaha appeared on the western bank of the Swami Pushkarini, while Venkateswara — Srinivasa — dwells on its southern bank. That is why at Tirumala the tradition is to have the darshan of Varaha Swami first.

About the Pictures

In this book Srinivasa's form is kept the same in every picture — deep dark blue-black, a tall gold crown, conch and discus, a blessing hand, his left hand on his hip, and a great white namam on his face. Vishnu in Vaikuntha is different from him — sky-blue, with a peacock feather in his crown. Lakshmi and Padmavati both wear red sarees — Padmavati is shown looking like Lakshmi, but she is Padmavati, not Lakshmi.
